definition: The program whose whole job is listening to your keyboard in a terminal. It reads each line, decides what you meant, and runs it — a translator between you and your computer, not magic.
The window where you type commands. Once a physical device, now an app that pretends to be one — the shell lives inside it.
The global system of interconnected computer networks, together with the physical links between them, that carries data between devices.
Short for World Wide Web: a system of interlinked hypertext documents and other resources, addressed by URLs and transferred over HTTP, that runs as a service on top of the internet.

A small, independently addressed unit of data — typically a few hundred to about 1,500 bytes — carrying a slice of a message plus a header describing where it came from, where it is going, and how to reassemble it.
A numerical address assigned to a device on a network so that packets can be routed to it.

The first widely deployed version of the Internet Protocol: 32-bit addresses written as four decimal numbers between 0 and 255, giving about 4.3 billion possible addresses — a pool that ran out in 2011.
The current version of the Internet Protocol: 128-bit addresses written in hexadecimal, providing an address supply large enough that exhaustion is no longer a practical concern.

Transmission Control Protocol: a transport protocol that provides reliable, ordered delivery of a stream of bytes over a connection, by acknowledging received packets, re-sending lost ones, and putting out-of-order arrivals back in sequence.
User Datagram Protocol: a transport protocol that sends datagrams with no handshake, no acknowledgement, and no re-sending, trading reliability for speed.
A device that forwards packets between networks, choosing the path each one takes toward its destination.
Network Address Translation: the technique of rewriting the source or destination address in packets as they pass through, letting many private devices share a single public IP address.
The packet-switching research network funded by the US Department of Defense's Advanced Research Projects Agency and switched on in 1969 — the direct ancestor of the internet.
Any program or device that initiates a request and receives the response.
Any program or device that listens for requests and responds to them.

An arrangement in which one party, the client, always initiates requests and the other, the server, always waits for and answers them. The relationship is asymmetric: only one side starts the conversation.
A message sent by a client asking a server to perform an action or return a resource, containing a method, a target, headers, and optionally a body.
A message sent by a server in reply to a request, containing a status code, headers, and usually a body.
The hostname that always refers to the machine the program is running on, reached over an internal loopback interface that never touches a network.
A network model in which every participant acts as both client and server, exchanging resources directly with peers and depending on no central server.
A client that performs little computation itself, relying on the server to do the work and return a largely finished result.
A client that performs most of the application's work itself, receiving data from the server and assembling the interface on its own.

HyperText Transfer Protocol: the application-layer protocol that defines how clients and servers exchange messages on the web, including the shape of a request, the shape of a response, and the meaning of the methods and status codes inside them.
HTTP transmitted over a TLS-encrypted connection. The message format is unchanged; the entire conversation is confidential and tamper-resistant.

A token in the request line of an HTTP request that indicates the desired action to be performed on the target resource. The standard methods are GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS, TRACE, and CONNECT.

A three-digit integer in the response status line that summarises the outcome of the request, grouped into five classes: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, and 5xx server error.

A key: value line in an HTTP message carrying metadata about the message or the entity it describes — who is asking, what formats are acceptable, how the body is encoded, or how long the response may be cached.
The payload of an HTTP message: the bytes actually being transferred, whose type and size are declared by the Content-Type and Content-Length headers. Optional in a request, usual in a response.

Uniform Resource Locator: a string that identifies a resource on the web and names the scheme by which to retrieve it, composed of a protocol, a domain, a path, an optional query string, and an optional fragment.

Transport Layer Security: the cryptographic protocol that provides confidentiality, integrity, and server authentication for a connection. The successor to SSL, standardised in 1999 as TLS 1.0, now at TLS 1.3.
Secure Sockets Layer: the encryption protocol Netscape developed in the 1990s and the direct ancestor of TLS. Deprecated because of vulnerabilities, but its name survives in everyday speech.

A digitally signed document, issued by a certificate authority, that binds a public key to a domain name. A client validates it during the TLS handshake to confirm it is talking to the server it intended to reach.
A defined mapping between numbers and characters, specifying which byte sequence represents which character in a text.

A variable-length character encoding that can represent every character in Unicode. Each character occupies one to four bytes: ASCII characters take one byte, most other scripts take two or three, and emoji take four.
The declared character encoding of a document's bytes, named in the charset parameter of a Content-Type header.
Text corruption caused by decoding a byte sequence with the wrong character encoding, so each byte is mapped to a character other than the one intended.
The four-step pattern of every HTTP exchange: the client sends a request, the server processes it, the server returns a response, and the client receives it.
Domain Name System: the distributed, hierarchical naming system that resolves human-readable domain names into IP addresses, with caches at every level to keep repeat lookups fast.
The three-message exchange — SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK — that establishes a TCP connection before any application data is sent.
Another name for the TCP handshake: three messages, one round trip, one open connection.
The negotiation that runs after the TCP connection is open, in which the server proves its identity with a certificate and both sides derive shared encryption keys.
The delay between sending a request and receiving a response, usually dominated by round-trip time; distance, handshakes, and server processing all add to it.
One complete journey of a message to the server and a reply back. Handshakes are priced in round trips.
A stored copy of a response or resource, held close to the requester so the request can be answered without repeating the full journey.
Time To First Byte: the elapsed time between sending a request and receiving the first byte of the response — the boundary between the connection phase and the server's processing phase.
An HTTP method that requests a representation of the specified resource. Safe and idempotent.
An HTTP method that submits data to the specified resource, often causing a change in state or the creation of a new resource. Neither safe nor idempotent.
An HTTP method that replaces all current representations of the target resource with the request payload. Not safe, but idempotent.
An HTTP method that applies partial modifications to a resource. Not safe, and not guaranteed to be idempotent. Standardised in RFC 5789.
An HTTP method that deletes the target resource. Not safe, but idempotent.
An HTTP method identical to GET except that the server must not return a message body. Safe and idempotent.
An HTTP method that requests information about the communication options available for the target resource. Safe and idempotent.
An HTTP method whose defined semantics are read-only: the client does not request, and does not expect, any change to the state of the server. The safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, and TRACE.

A property of an HTTP method where multiple identical requests have the same intended effect on the server as a single request, so a client can safely retry after a timeout. From the Latin idem (same) + potens (power).
Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four fundamental operations on persistent data, and the vocabulary every API ends up mapping onto HTTP methods.
Representational State Transfer — an architectural style for APIs, described by Roy Fielding in 2000, in which HTTP methods carry the action and URLs name resources.
A three-digit integer in the status line of an HTTP response that indicates the outcome of the request, defined by the HTTP specification and maintained in a public registry by IANA.
The standard response for a successful HTTP request; the meaning depends on the method: for GET it is the resource, for POST the result of the action.
The request succeeded and a new resource was created, usually with a Location header pointing to the new resource.
The request succeeded, but there is no body to return.
The target resource has been assigned a new permanent URI; clients should update their references.
The target resource resides temporarily under a different URI.
The resource has not been modified since the version the client already has, so the client should use its cached copy.
Like 302, but guarantees the request method will not change on the redirected request.
Like 301, but guarantees the request method will not change on the redirected request.
The server cannot process the request due to a client error, such as malformed syntax.
The client has not provided valid authentication credentials; the request lacks proven identity.
The server understood the request but refuses to authorize it; identity may be proven but permission is denied.
The server cannot find a current representation for the target resource, or is not willing to disclose that one exists.
The method specified in the request-line is not allowed for the target resource.
The request conflicts with the current state of the target resource.
The request is well-formed but contains semantically invalid data.
The client has sent too many requests in a given amount of time, typically accompanied by a Retry-After header.
The server encountered an unexpected condition that prevented it from fulfilling the request.
The server, acting as a gateway or proxy, received an invalid response from an upstream server.
The server is currently unable to handle the request due to overload or maintenance.
The server, acting as a gateway or proxy, did not receive a timely response from an upstream server.
